cases.title: Homes Taken for Xi'an Ring Roads and the Weiyang Palace Road, With Payments Left Late
cases.place: Weiyang Palace site in the Han Chang'an City area and the Second Ring Road interchange at Xinjiamiao, Weiyang District, Xi'an, Shaanxi, with further works in Huxian (Huyi) District, China
cases.point: The Han Chang'an City Weiyang Palace national archaeological site park, Weiyang District, Xi'an, where the project rebuilt a Han Dynasty road network and where 37 households were still waiting for replacement housing when the loan closed (OpenStreetMap point for the Weiyang Palace archaeological park)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-75580 for the Xi'an Sustainable Urban Transport Project (P092631). US$150 million, approved 24 June 2008, effective 24 December 2008, fully disbursed. Environmental category A. Original closing 30 June 2015; actual closing 31 March 2017 after two restructurings, on 22 December 2014 and 30 June 2016. The completion report's restructuring table gives the reason for the second restructuring as 'Delayed resettlement of 76 households' and records that the closing date was extended by nine months 'to allow completion of the resettlement'. The loan financed improvements to Xi'an's First and Second Ring Roads and Taibai Nan Road, the upgrading of four roads in Huxian, two passenger transport terminals and a bus depot, an area traffic control system, an air quality monitoring centre and laboratory, the re-creation of a Han Dynasty road network in the Weiyang Palace area and bicycle routes linking tourist sites. The project ran to 47 sub-components and 114 contracts at appraisal, 87 in the end. The completion report of 20 September 2017 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory, with quality at entry Moderately Unsatisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review, dated 5 March 2018 in the Bank's archive record, also reached Moderately Satisfactory on outcome, on a split rating of moderately unsatisfactory before the 2015 restructuring and moderately satisfactory after, weighted 40/60 by disbursement to 3.6; it rated risk to development outcome Modest and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00004130, 20 September 2017; Independent Evaluation Group ICR Review, CN-Xi'an Sustainable Urban Transport).

companies.name: Xi'an Project Management Office
companies.role: The implementing agency named in the completion report's data sheet. It coordinated eleven Xi'an municipal bodies listed in the completion report: the Development and Reform Commission, Finance Bureau, Planning Bureau, Construction Bureau, Environmental Protection Bureau, Communication Bureau, Civil Administration Bureau, National Land and Resources Bureau, Cultural Heritage Bureau and Public Security Bureau, together with the Xi'an Infrastructure Implementation Corporation. A separate project management office in Huxian handled the four county road sub-components; the completion report records weaknesses in its financial management system (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 20 September 2017).

cases.community: The project widened and rebuilt ring roads and interchanges across Xi'an and built a Han Dynasty road network inside the Weiyang Palace archaeological area. The completion report gives the outcome of the land take: 918,700 square metres of land, or 1,378 mu, was acquired, 152,000 square metres (228 mu) less than originally planned, and 99,945 square metres of houses and buildings were demolished. A total of 2,371 households, 11,433 people, were resettled under the project. The report states this is significantly more than the 527 households and 4,770 people estimated at appraisal, and attributes the difference to changes in the project design. Payments to 39 households in Xinjiamiao village and to 37 households at the Weiyang Palace construction site were delayed, and the completion report says those delays caused the second extension of the loan closing date. The 39 households at Xinjiamiao took monetary compensation and were paid in full by 31 December 2016. The 37 households at the Weiyang Palace site chose new housing rather than cash and were left waiting for the resettlement site to be built; the completion report, written in September 2017, says they would continue to receive transition subsidies until they moved to their permanent houses and that they would move no later than March 2018. That is more than nine months after the loan closed on 31 March 2017. The report rates social safeguards implementation Moderately Satisfactory and says the resettlement plan and policy framework were complied with. It also records that the project's one-year and nine-month closing extensions were needed to finish the resettlement, and that the project's appraisal underestimated the scale of resettlement required. The Evaluation Group's review repeats the same figures and adds that the Bank team may have underestimated the risk that resettlement posed to timely implementation.
cases.displaced_label: people resettled under the project, 2,371 households in all (World Bank completion report, 20 September 2017)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,100 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved; no figure of 2,100 was found in any Bank document opened. The Bank's completion report gives an outcome of 2,371 households, 11,433 people, resettled, against an appraisal estimate of 527 households and 4,770 people. The 11,433 is an outcome figure in the completion report, not a reprint of the appraisal plan, and the report itself sets the two side by side.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 31 March 2017 with 37 households at the Weiyang Palace site still in transitional housing, due to move by March 2018. The completion report says monitoring and reporting were continuing to ensure that all households were resettled according to the resettlement action plan. No document found records whether the 37 households moved on that date. A follow-up Bank operation, the Shaanxi Xi'an Intelligent Public Transport Project (P157787), was under preparation when the completion report was written.

The lender is reporting on its own project. No independent press account, court record, audit or field study of this resettlement was found; two searches, one of them in Chinese for the named village, returned nothing on these works. The completion report names no affected person, gives no compensation rate, does not say how long the payments to the 39 and the 37 households were late, and does not break the 11,433 people down by site. It states that the resettlement plan and policy framework were complied with and rates social safeguards implementation Moderately Satisfactory. The completion report gives risk to development outcome as Moderate and the Evaluation Group's review gives it as Modest; the review records no disagreement with the report on this rating and the reasons it gives for it are favourable throughout. The Evaluation Group's review prints no date anywhere on the page; the date given for it is the Bank archive's own record field, which is not verified on the document itself.
cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered the policies on environmental assessment, physical cultural resources and involuntary resettlement. The Project Agreement for Loan 7558-CN, dated 29 September 2008, required the implementing entity, where acquisition of land or assets or displacement of people was unavoidable, to make compensation available in accordance with the resettlement action plans and the resettlement policy framework 'before the carrying out of the works which would result in such acquisition or displacement', in a manner satisfactory to the Bank. It also barred amendment, suspension or waiver of the plans without the Bank's prior concurrence, and made activities under three parts of the project ineligible for financing unless a resettlement action plan for them had been prepared under the policy framework and approved by the Bank. The completion report records that payments to 39 households at Xinjiamiao and 37 at the Weiyang Palace site were delayed, and that the delay forced the nine-month extension of the closing date (Project Agreement, 29 September 2008; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 20 September 2017).

cases.title: Years in Transitional Housing for Families Moved Off the Jiefang Avenue Extension
cases.place: Nanhu Village resettlement site, Huangpi District, Wuhan, Hubei, with works also on the Jiefang Avenue Extension and the Shuidong section of the Second Ring Road, China
cases.point: Huangpi District, Wuhan, the district that built and was responsible for the Nanhu Village resettlement site and whose approval delays left families in transitional housing (OpenStreetMap administrative point for Huangpi District; the village itself is not mapped at a point that could be confirmed)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-78640 for the Wuhan Second Urban Transport Project (P112838). US$100 million, approved 30 March 2010, effective 7 September 2010, fully disbursed. Environmental category B. Original closing 31 December 2015; actual closing 31 August 2018 after restructurings on 26 June 2015 and 30 August 2017. Total project cost rose from US$610.71 million at appraisal to US$926.82 million, the borrower's own contribution rising from US$510.71 million to US$826.82 million. The loan financed the Jiefang Avenue Extension, the elevated and ground sections of the Shuidong stretch of the Second Ring Road, the Tianshunyuan and Sanjintan public transport terminals and bus corridor works. The completion report of 28 June 2019 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and quality of monitoring and evaluation Modest. The Independent Evaluation Group's review, dated 18 November 2019 in the Bank's archive record, recommended the project for a field-based assessment alongside two other Chinese urban transport projects (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2019; Independent Evaluation Group ICR Review, CN-Wuhan Second Urban Transport).

companies.name: Wuhan Urban Construction Utilization of Foreign Investment Project Management Office
companies.role: The implementing agency named in the completion report's data sheet, the unit of the Wuhan municipal construction administration that handles foreign-financed urban works. Land acquisition and resettlement were not run from it: the completion report states the resettlement work was subproject and district based and was carried out by the acquisition and compensation departments of the district in which each subproject sat, with Huangpi District in charge of building the Nanhu Village resettlement site (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2019).

companies.name: Center for Involuntary Resettlement Research, Wuhan University
companies.role: The independent monitor required by the resettlement action plan. It monitored the project's resettlement work and submitted 16 external monitoring reports to the Bank between January 2011 and July 2018 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2019). None of those 16 reports was found in the Bank's document archive.

cases.community: The project built the Jiefang Avenue Extension and the Shuidong section of Wuhan's Second Ring Road, with works scattered across the city. The completion report records that 7 urban residential communities and 21 suburban villages were affected in various degrees by land acquisition and house demolition, that the project affected 1,055 families with 3,265 people and 40 enterprises, and that it required 31 hectares of land and nearly 300,000 square metres of structures. The resettlement plan was updated for the Nanhu Village Interchange sub-project of the Jiefang Avenue Extension, with a demolition area of 116,700 square metres, which the report says made this the largest-scale resettlement among the Bank's transport projects in China at the time. Three resettlement sites were used, and the report's account of them differs sharply by site. At the Shuidong section, all displaced families received full compensation, annual village royalty payments from village business profits, several apartments each on average, and social security and medical insurance as they became urban residents. On the Jiefang Avenue section, where some displaced families included laid-off workers and some were below the urban poverty line, the resettlement works took over six years until every displaced family was relocated to their new apartments. At the Jiefang Avenue Extension section, Huangpi District was in charge of the Nanhu Village resettlement site, 1,500 apartments serving this project and three municipally funded projects. The land approval, design and urban planning of that site were delayed for over three years because the area had been taken into a new city, the Yangtze River Eco-city, approved by the State Council in 2016, which voided the earlier land-use planning. Without fresh land-use approval, the site's electricity, drinking water and gas could not be connected to the mains, and a plant to treat the new city's wastewater was still outstanding when the report was written. Resettlement at Nanhu Village was still unfinished when the loan closed on 31 August 2018 and when the completion report was written in June 2019; Huangpi District was paying the residents the stipulated transition fee. The report says the residents were aware of the delay and their entitlements and had expressed their understanding of the situation. Escalating land acquisition and resettlement costs ran through the project: the cost rose from US$192 million estimated at appraisal to US$520 million, an increase the completion report puts at 183.6 per cent and attributes mostly to rising real estate prices in Wuhan and in China generally. The Evaluation Group's review records that the shortage of counterpart funds to pay those costs delayed the Jiefang Avenue Extension and that the second extension of the closing date was due to slow resettlement in Huangpi District and delayed land acquisition for the two public transport terminals. The Bank's own grievance redress service received no complaints from citizens, and the final Bank supervision mission in March 2019 concluded that social safeguards were Satisfactory.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,486 for this project. That is the appraisal plan figure: the Project Appraisal Document of 2 March 2010 states that 'Housing demolition will entail the relocation of 391 households with 1,486 people, 218 shops (with 556 employees), and 21 enterprises'. It is not a count of people moved. The completion report's outcome figures are larger in households and structures and smaller in land: 1,055 families with 3,265 people and 40 enterprises affected, 31 hectares of land against 48.2 hectares planned, and nearly 300,000 square metres of structures. The completion report's verb for the 1,055 families is 'affected', not relocated, and no Bank document found gives a count of people actually relocated, either in total or at any one of the three resettlement sites.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 31 August 2018 with the Nanhu Village resettlement unfinished. The project management office and the Bank agreed that resettlement would be monitored every three months and that all families would be relocated to their new housing by June 2020, with the Bank monitoring that under a later operation, the Wuhan Integrated Transport Development Project. No document found records whether the families moved by that date. The Evaluation Group recommended the project for a field-based assessment; no Project Performance Assessment Report for it was found in the Bank's archive.

The lender is reporting on its own project. No independent account of the Nanhu Village resettlement was found; two searches, one of them in Chinese for the village and the road, returned nothing on these works. The 16 external monitoring reports the completion report relies on are not in the Bank's public archive, so the figures cannot be checked against them. The report does not say how many families were at the Nanhu Village site, how many were still in transitional housing when the loan closed, how long any one family waited, or what the transition fee was. It states that the residents had expressed their understanding of the delay, that the Bank's grievance service received no complaints, and that the final supervision mission rated social safeguards Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group's review prints no date anywhere on the page; the date given for it is the Bank archive's own record field, which is not verified on the document itself.
cases.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered the policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. The Project Agreement for Loan 7864-CN, dated 11 June 2010, required Wuhan, where acquisition of land or assets or displacement of people was unavoidable, to do two things 'before initiating the implementation of any works which would result in such acquisition or displacement': make compensation available and, as applicable, 'relocate and rehabilitate the displaced people in permanent sites with adequate facilities, including providing all related assistance required in respect thereof', in accordance with the resettlement action plan; and, where the relocation and rehabilitation assistance provided was of a transitory nature, 'make arrangements prior to implementing any such works for the permanent and adequate relocation and rehabilitation of such people in accordance with the RAP', on a time schedule satisfactory to the Bank. A further clause required Wuhan to carry out measures satisfactory to the Bank for improving the living standard of displaced persons. The completion report records that at the Nanhu Village site the electricity, drinking water and gas could not be connected, that the site's approvals were delayed for over three years, and that resettlement there was still outstanding when the loan closed and when the report was written ten months later (Project Agreement, 11 June 2010; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 June 2019).

cases.title: Households Relocated for the Qingyang Ring Roads as Resettlement Costs Tripled
cases.place: Xifeng District, Qingyang, Gansu, China
cases.point: Xifeng District, the Qingyang city district holding all six sub-projects in the completion report's land acquisition table (OpenStreetMap place point for Xifeng District, Qingyang)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-81700 for the Gansu Qingyang Urban Infrastructure Improvement Project (P123133). US$100 million, approved 31 May 2012, effective 24 September 2012, fully disbursed. Environmental category B. Original closing 31 December 2017; actual closing 30 November 2019 after restructurings on 23 August 2016 and 10 October 2018. The loan financed urban roads in Xifeng District - the west section of Anding Road, the middle and south sections of Qinghua Road forming the west ring road, the north section of Beijing Road forming the east ring road and the east section of Guxiang Lu - together with the Dongqu wastewater treatment plant, drainage and wastewater management and transport action plans. The completion report of 21 May 2020 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and quality of monitoring and evaluation Modest; the Independent Evaluation Group's review, dated 10 November 2020 in the Bank's archive record, reached the same three ratings (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 21 May 2020; Independent Evaluation Group ICR Review, CN-Gansu Qingyang Urban Infrastructure).

companies.name: Qingyang Project Management Office
companies.role: The implementing agency named in the completion report's data sheet. Under the project agreement the loan was made available through Gansu province to Qingyang Municipality and Xifeng District, with a project implementation unit in the Xifeng Housing bureau and another in the municipal water company. The municipal resettlement office supervised land acquisition and resettlement (Project Appraisal Document, 30 April 2012; Project Agreement for Loan 8170-CN, 12 July 2012; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 21 May 2020).

companies.name: Qingyang Municipal Water Supply and Sewage Company
companies.role: The municipal utility responsible for the wastewater component, one of the six sub-projects in the land acquisition table. The project included a covenant requiring it to furnish a financial performance improvement plan and to break even; the completion report records late delivery of that plan and an operating ratio of less than one (Project Appraisal Document, 30 April 2012; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 21 May 2020).

cases.community: The project built ring roads and a wastewater treatment plant on the edge of Xifeng District, the city district of Qingyang. The completion report sets out the outcome in a table of land acquisition and resettlement by sub-project: 800.66 mu of land acquired permanently, 324.1 mu occupied temporarily, 2,149 households affected and 226 households relocated. The relocations fell on three of the six sub-projects: 14 households on the west section of Anding Road, 114 on the north section of Beijing Road, 90 on the south section of Qinghua Road and 8 at the Dongqu wastewater works. The report also records that 640 households affected by house demolition and the removal of attachments were paid RMB466.3 million, that RMB53.27 million was paid to affected villages and individuals for permanent acquisition and temporary occupation together, and that the total cost of land acquisition and resettlement came to RMB520 million, 229 per cent more than the estimate in the resettlement action plan. A church and 35 household graves were relocated during road construction. The design of the street on West Anding Road was changed to avoid resettling an elderly landlord who refused to move and who, a photograph caption in the report says, refused any compensation plan. The resettlement ran years behind: by March 2015 only one of the project's 10 civil works contracts had completed land acquisition and resettlement, because land approvals given by Qingyang Municipality were not valid under a new land policy and had to be escalated to provincial level, and an audit of the municipal land bureau suspended the issue of land preview notes. Once the approvals came, the availability of local funds to pay for the resettlement became an issue alongside the growing cost. The 2016 restructuring cancelled two sub-projects - the final kilometre of the Western Ring Road and the purchase of vehicle equipment - to relieve the pressure on counterpart financing created by the rise in resettlement costs. The completion report also states that all affected households of the six sub-projects signed compensation agreements, received compensation and have been rehabilitated, that all temporarily occupied land was restored and returned, that ten monitoring reports concluded the resettlement plan was implemented satisfactorily and all affected people received the compensation due to them, and that a sample survey by the external monitoring team found the income and living conditions of affected people improved significantly after resettlement. The Evaluation Group's review puts it as 'the project affected 2,149 households, and 226 households were satisfactorily relocated'.
cases.displaced_label: households relocated, from the "Number of Relocated households" column of Table 4 (World Bank completion report, 21 May 2020)
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,800 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved; no figure of 1,800 was found in any Bank document opened. The appraisal document estimated 740 mu of permanent land acquisition in eight villages in five townships, affecting 201 families or 862 people by land acquisition and 143 families by structure demolition; the appraisal gives the people in those 143 families as 528 in one passage and 529 in another. The completion report's outcome figures are larger throughout: 800.66 mu acquired, 2,149 households affected, 640 households affected by house demolition and attachment removal, and 226 households relocated. No Bank document found converts the 226 relocated households into a number of people.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 November 2019 with the roads and the wastewater plant built and the resettlement complete. The completion report records that the plant's capacity had been miscalculated and that an emergency 10,000 cubic metre pool was to be built south of it before the 2020 rainy season to handle emergencies. The two cancelled sub-projects were not built with Bank money.

A resettlement action plan was prepared, reviewed and disclosed before appraisal, advertised in local newspapers, posted on the Qingyang government website and held at the Qingyang Municipal Library free of charge. cases.title: Houses Pulled Down Three Years Before the Replacement Flats Were Built in Xining
cases.place: Taobei, Wangjiazhai and Wuzhong villages and the Wusixi Road and Xicheng Avenue corridor, Chengbei District, Xining, with works also in Huangzhong County, Qinghai, China
cases.point: Chengbei District, Xining, the district in which the completion report says the entire project was located and in which the Taobei and Wangjiazhai resettlement complexes were built (OpenStreetMap administrative point for Chengbei District)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-83190 for the Qinghai Xining Urban Transport Project (P127867). US$120 million, approved 27 December 2013, effective 21 May 2014, revised to US$115,551,102 and that amount disbursed. Environmental category B. Original closing 30 September 2019; actual closing 30 August 2021 after restructurings on 26 September 2019 and 27 May 2021. Total project cost US$228,381,102, of which the borrower provided US$112,830,000. The loan financed new urban roads on the Wusixi Road corridor - Xicheng Avenue, 3.64 km with three bridges and an underpass; Wusixi Road, 3.43 km; and No. 5 Road, 1.02 km - dedicated bus lanes, stops and a public transport interchange, buses, an area traffic control system and studies and training. The 2019 restructuring added upgrades to Qiyi, Delingha, Bayi and Wuyi roads, 73 electric bus charging points and a relocated passenger station, and moved the public transport interchange from Yanxiaocun to Wangjiazhai. The completion report states flatly that 'The project did not finance land acquisision'; the city put US$83.7 million of its own counterpart funding into resettlement-related activities. The completion report of 22 February 2022 rated outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and quality of monitoring and evaluation Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 29 June 2022 reached the same three ratings (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00005538, 22 February 2022; Independent Evaluation Group ICR Review, China - Qinghai Xining Urban Transport Project).

companies.name: Xining Municipal Government
companies.role: The implementing agency named in the completion report's data sheet, working through a project management office. The completion report records that the Chengbei district government provided guidance and support in obtaining upper-level approvals for urban planning and urban land use and monitored the quality of the resettlement apartment construction, and that village committees ran much of the resettlement work - the impact survey, the collection of farmers' concerns, choosing the designer of the resettlement sites, organising their construction, and distributing apartments to affected families (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 22 February 2022).

companies.name: Xining Chengtong Transportation Construction & Investment Co., Ltd.
companies.role: The project implementing unit, the Xining municipal investment company that coordinated the January 2018 field survey and public consultation for the updated resettlement action plan (Resettlement Action Plan, January 2018).

companies.name: Involuntary Resettlement Research Center, China Three Gorges University
companies.role: The resettlement consulting agency that carried out the field survey and public consultation for the updated resettlement action plan between 7 and 20 January 2018 (Resettlement Action Plan, January 2018).

cases.community: The project built new roads and a bus corridor across the northern edge of Xining. The appraisal document described two kinds of land take. The first was work treated as relevant to the project but carried out before the project was identified: a due diligence review covered the demolition of 520,487 square metres of houses, the acquisition of 368 hectares of land and the resettlement of 760 households during 2010 to 2012, and concluded those activities followed Chinese land law and Qinghai provincial and local regulation, with living conditions restored. The second was the land take for the project itself. The appraisal estimated 52.8 hectares of land across six villages in Chengbei District and Huangzhong County, 481 households and 1,921 people affected by land acquisition, the demolition of 150,661 square metres of structures displacing 121 households and 527 people, and the demolition of a further 5,792 square metres in seven enterprises. The updated resettlement action plan of January 2018 gives the outcome, citing the external monitoring agency's report: the land acquisition and structure demolition of the project had all been completed by 31 December 2016, with 233,600 square metres of structures demolished and 724.88 mu of land acquired, excluding the passenger station. The same document then records that the construction of the resettlement complexes was about three years later than the original plan. Construction of the Taobei Village resettlement complex was only started in October 2017, that of the Wangjiazhai Village complex in November 2017, and that of the Huangzhong County complex had not yet been started at all when the plan was written in January 2018 - more than a year after the houses came down. The completion report, written four years later, states that all resettlement sites were completed before the loan closed, that each family received at least two apartments, that villagers live in the same community without disruption to their original neighbourhoods, and that savings from building the resettlement sites were used to set up village enterprises paying the villagers a yearly share. It also records that the transitional fees for displaced families were first paid monthly, that this was not convenient for some of them, and that after an internal review the fees were changed to a yearly payment. Grievances were taken by the village committee, the district and the project office's resettlement agency, by telephone or in person. Individual family tombs along the road alignment were relocated; the Bank's cultural resources adviser agreed they had no archaeological, palaeontological, architectural, religious, aesthetic or cultural significance, and their relocation was handled under the resettlement policy rather than the cultural property policy. The Bank concluded that its policy on indigenous peoples did not apply: Xining has 38 ethnic minorities making up 26 per cent of its population, but in Chengbei District, where the completion report says the entire project was located, over 90 per cent of the population is Han.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,444 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The nearest figures in the Bank's documents are the appraisal estimates of 1,921 people in 481 households affected by land acquisition and 527 people in 121 households displaced by housing demolition, which come to 2,448; no document found states 2,444. The completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review both reprint the appraisal's 121 households and 527 individuals, and both keep the appraisal's forward-looking verb - the Evaluation Group writes that the project's investments 'involved displacing 121 households (527 individuals)'. Neither gives an outcome count of anyone moved. The outcome figures that do exist are areas, in the updated resettlement action plan of January 2018: 233,600 square metres of structures demolished and 724.88 mu of land acquired by 31 December 2016, against 150,661 square metres and 788.09 mu planned. No Bank document found gives a count of people or households actually relocated under the project.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 August 2021. The completion report says all three resettlement complexes were finished before closing and that each family received at least two apartments. The gap between the demolition, finished on 31 December 2016, and the start of the last complex, which had not begun in January 2018, is recorded only in the updated resettlement action plan; neither the completion report nor the Independent Evaluation Group's review mentions the delay or says when the Huangzhong County complex was finished.

The report says these impacts were slightly higher than planned, on the basis of detailed measurements taken during implementation. The Evaluation Group's review prints a table of planned against actual figures that the Bank's project team supplied to the evaluators because the units differed between the appraisal document and the completion report. It gives the land take as 2,241.9 mu planned against 2,913 acquired, an increase of 30 per cent, of which arable land rose from 383.75 mu to 506.52, an increase of 32 per cent; and the demolition as 16 households planned against 21, 5,760 square metres against 7,708 and 76 people against 96, increases of 31, 34 and 26 per cent. The reasons the table gives are local design changes, lighting construction, the acquisition of small parcels left over after the main take, arable land left inaccessible behind the airport, and land reserved for military requirements. At appraisal the figures had been 150 hectares of village land, including 26 hectares of cultivated land, affecting some 2,500 people from 500 households, and the demolition of 5,760 square metres of structures affecting 76 people from 16 households. Resettlement activities started in 2013 and were completed by the end of 2018, the month the loan closed. Field surveys found 137 household graves on the airport site; their relocation was compensated under the resettlement action plan. The project also interrupted local rural roads and irrigation systems, which the resettlement plan covered, and the appraisal noted that noise from the airport in operation might be unavoidable for local people. Both documents report the outcome favourably. The completion report says resettlement monitoring showed affected people have better housing, including better infrastructure such as water, drainage and community services, and that semi-annual external monitoring confirmed land acquisition and compensation were carried out in accordance with the resettlement plans. The Evaluation Group's review adds that there were no delays in the payment of appropriate compensation. A 2016 consultant survey of 30 affected households in Zunqiao town, the town the completion report says was most affected by resettlement, found that between 2013 and 2015 average household income rose from RMB28,534 to RMB35,950, a growth of 26 per cent, average household living area rose from 388 to 472 square metres, and the share of agriculture in average household income fell from 12.9 to 10.4 per cent, which the report reads as affected villagers moving out of farming into airport work. The 4.65 km access road linking the airport to the nearest main road was built by the municipal government outside the project, and was brought inside the resettlement action plan for safeguards purposes.

companies.role: The state company that ran the works as the project implementation entity and commissioned the end-of-term evaluation of resettlement for the Dimitrovgrad bypass. The company gave no official response to N1's questions in November 2016; its representatives had visited the village and promised that all damage would be compensated once blasting was finally over.

companies.name: Public Enterprise Roads of Serbia
companies.role: The state road enterprise, named in the completion report as PEPS and in the evaluation as PERS, which was the beneficiary of the expropriation and the owner of the acquired land, and which held the individual expropriation case files and valuation reports.

cases.community: The loan paid for motorway sections on Corridor X, including the bypass around Dimitrovgrad on the E-80 towards the Bulgarian border. The appraisal document of 12 June 2009 expected expropriation on the Bank-financed sections of 50 hectares on Grabovnica-Grdelica, 130 hectares on Vladicin Han-Donji Neradovac and 50 hectares on the 8.67 kilometres around Dimitrovgrad, 230 hectares in all. The completion report records land acquisition of 322.7 hectares across 2,092 cases on those three sections, rising to 371.8 hectares and 2,491 cases once Lot 6 was added, and says there were delays in complying with the resettlement action plans because of the slow expropriation process in 2011-2012 and in 2015, caused by a lack of expropriation funds, disputes over expropriation, and delays in paying subsistence and transitional allowances to displaced families. It states that the expropriation process for the whole project was substantially completed by 2016 and that the handling of expropriation impacts was consistent with the Bank-endorsed plans and complied with the resettlement policy. An end-of-term impact evaluation of resettlement on the Dimitrovgrad bypass, dated 12 July 2016, goes further. The resettlement action plan recorded 33 structures expropriated and compensated on that section; the road enterprise's own records held 30 cases, the difference being that some cases bundled a house with its wells, fences and storage. Thirteen cases included houses and only three of those involved physical relocation: six of the seven residential structures recorded at Dimitrovgrad were weekend houses, one house was derelict with nobody living in it, and three of the six houses at Gradinje were weekend homes. The evaluation interviewed representatives of two of the three physically displaced households. One had bought a new house, smaller than the old one, with compensation of RSD 7,630,169, about EUR 85,000, covering a 4,497 square metre plot and the structures, and the evaluation judged that adequate and above local market prices. The second, who declined to take part, had received about EUR 70,000 for structures. In neither case was there evidence that the moving allowance the law prescribes or the transitional allowance the resettlement policy framework requires had been paid. The third case was a household and a business together. Vasil Kolev had a 140 square metre building at Gradinje with a registered car repair workshop on the ground floor and the family home above; it was fully expropriated and the replacement value was assessed at about EUR 27,000, or EUR 160 a square metre. He was notified in 2008, was not satisfied with the valuation, and says the authorities did not respond to his appeal to reassess. He received no moving allowance, no transitional allowance and no compensation for loss of business or loss of income; the valuation covered the construction value of the workshop only, so the equipment in it was not valued, and he removed it himself at his own cost. Losing the workshop left the household without its only source of income. He was 60 at the time of the interview, worked part time as a handyman, and lived with his wife, disabled from birth, and a daughter trained as a hairdresser but not in full-time work. He said property prices in Dimitrovgrad had risen since the expropriation began and he could not buy a new property, and that he lives in a house inherited from his father. The evaluation confirmed from the valuation report that only the construction value had been assessed, found that the basic requirements of the resettlement policy framework had not been met in his case, recommended that the outstanding allowances be paid retrospectively to the displaced households and that an independent review of his case be carried out, and noted that he had since claimed to have the property expropriated back because the building had never been demolished and a slight change to the carriageway alignment made demolition unlikely. The expropriation of these households was completed in Phase 1, in 2008 and 2009, before the international lenders came into the project. The appraisal document had said as much in advance about an adjoining stretch: expropriation on the first 5.9 kilometres from Prosek towards Crvena Reka began in late 2008 and, although the Bank reviewed the process, that section was not to be subject to the policies set out in the resettlement policy framework. The construction impacts were not. Negative impacts the affected people reported during the works were damage to local roads, limited access to land parcels, effects on the value of utilities, and blasting. The evaluation records the municipality's representatives as stating that over 100 households were affected to varying extents by the blasting and that about 20 households at Gradinje were severely affected. Eleven households had been identified as vulnerable when the resettlement plan was prepared and each received additional financial assistance of RSD 60,000. Court appeals were brought over compensation for lost crops; the evaluation found no records of how many crop expropriation cases there were, because all records sat in paper case files, and no information on the court cases or their outcomes, and concluded that the appeals were not non-compliance with the plan or a major impact. N1 reported on 24 November 2016 from the village of Gradina near Dimitrovgrad that construction was going on a few metres from houses, that it had run about five years, that houses had cracks inside and out which residents attributed to the blasting and the works, and that residents whose houses were damaged were waiting for compensation. It reported that residents had written to several authorities asking to be relocated, had written again the week before, and had threatened to block the blasting. One of them, Nebojsa Ivanov, said that experts had come and had said the building was not safe to live in, and that he would have to sue if he could not reach an agreement with Koridori Srbije. One resident, Nebojsa Ivanov, said: 'Nista ne kazu. Kao da ne postojimo' - they say nothing, as if we do not exist. Another resident, Slavka Gligorijev, said she was waiting for the works to end and did not know what would be done about the damaged houses. The report said at least five firms had worked on the section over the five years and residents had asked all of them for compensation, but the damage only grew; and that unofficially, expropriation would not happen at this stage and residents with damaged houses would have to wait for compensation until all work was finished. Koridori Srbije gave no official response. The evaluation's own view of the wider picture was that Dimitrovgrad remains one of the poorest municipalities in Serbia, that the affected people's perception of their economic position was negative but that they attributed the worsening to factors outside the project, and that there had been observable improvement in their socio-economic conditions since 2009, some of it from compensation money and construction jobs.

cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,337 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts 2,491 cases of affected landowners across 371.8 hectares for the whole project and gives no count of people relocated. The three is for the Dimitrovgrad bypass section alone, the only section with a published end-of-term resettlement evaluation; no equivalent count was found for the E-75 sections, where the completion report records delays in paying subsistence and transitional allowances to displaced families without saying how many families.
cases.suppression: Vasil Kolev told the evaluation's consultant that when he sought legal assistance from several lawyers, none of them would represent him, on the pretext that it is better not to go against the State. The evaluation reports this as his statement and does not name the lawyers or test the claim.
cases.killed_note: The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that there were three fatalities during highway construction. The completion report records three separate fatal accidents at the sites - in September 2013 at Grabovnica-Grdelica and in November 2014 and February 2017 at the Dimitrovgrad bypass - and attributes them to unsatisfactory management of site safety; a health and safety audit report and a site safety action plan were implemented for the first two and additional safety measures introduced for the third. The review says that apart from stating unsatisfactory management of site safety the completion report gives no detail on whether the safety measures were sufficient to protect construction workers, whether there was negligence, and whether the accidents could have been avoided. Neither document names the people killed or says what each accident was.
cases.outcome: The loan closed on 30 September 2019, almost four years after its original date, with the Bank-financed sections open to traffic. The end-of-term evaluation of 12 July 2016 recommended that the outstanding moving and transitional allowances be paid retrospectively to the displaced households, that an independent review of Vasil Kolev's case be carried out, that the scale of construction impacts on the community be verified and documented and that outstanding compensation be paid in full. On the blasting damage the evaluation records that compensation was being paid by the insurer Wiener Stadtische but that only five cases had been compensated by the time it was written and that the claim process was long, and that the damage to houses in and around Sutjeska Street in Dimitrovgrad was reimbursed for five households out of the contractor's bank guarantee on court decisions, with further cases pending in court. No document found records how many households were compensated in the end, whether the evaluation's recommendations were acted on, or how Vasil Kolev's claim to have the property expropriated back was resolved. The completion report of 24 March 2020 rated the outcome Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed, while downrating Bank performance to Moderately Satisfactory over the three construction deaths.

That is not an independent document: the evaluator was engaged by the implementing entity. N1's report of 24 November 2016 corroborates independently that houses near the works were cracked, that residents attributed this to blasting, and that compensation was being withheld until the works finished, and it names two residents, one of whom states that experts had found his building unsafe to live in. The report does not say who engaged those experts. N1 places its report in the village of Gradina while the evaluation's affected structures are at Gradinje and Dimitrovgrad; both villages lie on the same bypass section, and no document found states that they are the same place. The expropriation of the three displaced households, including the workshop, was completed in 2008 and 2009, before the international lenders joined the project; what falls inside the loan period is the construction impact, the Bank-endorsed resettlement framework under which the allowances were owed, and the evaluation's finding that they had not been paid. Vasil Kolev's account of his losses, and the statement that lawyers would not represent him, are his own, recorded by the evaluation's consultant, who confirmed from the valuation report only that the workshop had been valued for construction value alone and noted that no evidence was provided of how the business operated or how much income was lost. The completion report states the opposite conclusion on the same facts - that the handling of expropriation impacts complied with the resettlement policy - and the evaluation found the compensation paid to the displaced households adequate and above local market prices. The three construction deaths are counted by the Independent Evaluation Group; neither document names the people killed, says what happened in each accident, or says whether the deaths could have been avoided. No document found gives the number of households whose houses cracked or what they were paid in total; the evaluation records five cases compensated by the works insurer and five households compensated out of the contractor's bank guarantee on court decisions, with further cases pending. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 8 October 2020 date is the Bank's catalogue field and is unverified at document level.
cases.conditions: The project triggered Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP/BP 4.04) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12). A resettlement policy framework was prepared for the whole project and disclosed on 4 June 2009, with separate resettlement action plans for the Dimitrovgrad bypass (April 2010), Grabovnica-Grdelica (July 2011), Vladicin Han-Donji Neradovac (April 2012, with an annex in March 2014) and the Lot 6 Manajle-Vladicin Han tunnel (April 2014), and an addendum in May 2015. Two corridor-level environmental impact assessments covering the whole of E-75 and E-80 were cleared before appraisal in May 2009, with seven sub-section assessments for E-75 and five for E-80 consolidated into them, and site-specific environmental management plans issued with the bidding documents for each works contract. Serbian expropriation law requires affected structures to be compensated at full replacement cost, treats a partly affected structure as wholly expropriated, and provides for a moving allowance in cases of physical relocation but prescribes no transitional allowance; the resettlement policy framework required a transitional allowance as well. The end-of-term evaluation of 12 July 2016 found that the framework's basic requirements had not been met in the case of the affected business, that there was no evidence that the moving or transitional allowances had been paid to any of the three physically displaced households, and that the monitoring of construction impacts the resettlement plan required was not a priority in the contractors' obligations (End of Term Impact Evaluation of Resettlement, 12 July 2016; Implementation Completion and Results Report, 24 March 2020).

cases.community: The loan and credit paid for 26 kilometres of road between Milot and Rreshen, built in three lots and all open to traffic by the project's close. The completion report names the Milot-Rreshen section as the main project activity that triggered land acquisition, and records that a resettlement action plan was prepared by the road agency's project implementation team and approved by the Bank. Land was acquired in two rounds. After the first was finished, the Government enacted a new Law on Property Valuation in 2010, which changed how compensation was calculated and, in the completion report's words, 'led to a reduction in the rate of compensation paid to Project-affected persons'. The change was made to accommodate a redesign of the road alignment and an unrelated landslip in Fang village. The Bank team, after taking advice from its regional safeguards adviser and project lawyer, told the road agency it could apply the new law, and the resettlement action plan was changed accordingly. The report says the new law 'triggered some dissatisfaction from people who had gone through the first expropriation and then through the second'. Payment of compensation was also delayed. Some title holders were out of the country or had died with successors who held no title. The 2010 law required compensation to be paid through one named bank; most of the people affected by the construction works lived in the area where the flood protection works were built and were rural, and many had no bank account, so the report states that this provision 'significantly delayed payments of due compensations'. The project implementation team explained an alternative method of calculating compensation, had land registration offices give owners without titles preferential status, helped every owner open an account at the nearest branch of the designated bank in Milot, Rrubik or Rreshen, and opened an escrow account for those who had died or were abroad. Twenty-three households lost their homes and had to be relocated; all were compensated and assisted to settle in new places, and in one case where the residence was occupied without title the Municipality of Milot provided the family with a new apartment at no cost. A further 12 households lost their commercial structures in part or in whole. Three hundred and thirty-eight households lost agricultural or commercial land. Compensation for residential and commercial structures totalled ALL 174,165,661, about US$1.7 million, and compensation for agricultural and commercial land and for lost agricultural production and expected income in the year of taking and the two or three years after came to ALL 185,854,139, about US$1.8 million. cases.community: The loans paid for the first 40 kilometre phase of the Amman Ring Road, running from Zarqa, Amman's main industrial suburb, past Queen Alia International Airport, and for a new customs depot and inland port at Madounah. The completion report states that the scale of land acquisition required was far greater than any land acquisition programme previously carried out in Jordan. The number of people ultimately affected, defined as owners and occupants who lost some of their land, housing or other physical assets, was 3,028, and compensation payments amounted to about US$160 million equivalent, against the US$158.43 million the report's own cost table gives. Three quarters of the compensation, covering 440 hectares, 850 plots and 2,250 affected people, was for the 40 kilometre road route; one quarter, covering 500 hectares, 240 plots and 778 affected people, was for the Madounah areas selected in 2006 for the customs depot and inland port. The draft land acquisition and resettlement plan disclosed in February 2004 had indicated the road would affect about 500 plots with about 1,900 identified owners, the very large majority private parties. Particular attention was given to people considered vulnerable: female landowners, who were about a third of those identified; tenants; people dependent on customary rights, mainly herders whose livelihoods came almost entirely from the rangelands the road runs through; and the 300 or so owners and occupants who had to find new places for themselves and their dependents to live. Because the road was to be Jordan's first limited-access facility, the Government agreed to pay each owner for all the land taken rather than the 75 per cent that Jordanian law permits and that earlier public requisitions had applied. An independent monitor was appointed and reviewed the programme at the turn of 2006 and 2007, later than intended because of difficulty finding a suitable expert. She carried out physical and telephone interviews, reached broadly positive conclusions, called the approach 'an exemplary approach to be pursued in similar future projects', and identified areas for improvement, chiefly more follow-up with affected people after their land had been given up and better recording of their contacts with officials. In response the ministry's community liaison office interviewed a sample of affected people, especially women and those physically resettled. The completion report states that those interview reports 'record widespread concern particularly about the slow payment of compensation - with eight months seeming to be found often acceptable, but not periods well in excess of one year as seem to have arisen not too often but nonetheless more frequently than expected'. The period of compensation payment and resettlement, 2004 to 2008, coincided with large increases in the price of land and building materials, driven by oil price rises, the removal of earlier subsidies and the arrival of people fleeing the fighting in Iraq. Other interviews recorded the ministry responding flexibly to cases that risked severe harm: watering roads to reduce dust that was damaging olive harvests, building additional animal underpasses to reconnect herders' grazing lands, small changes to the road alignment to avoid taking small pieces of property, and measures to speed up payment to people in exceptional difficulty. At Madounah, the 500 hectares were acquired at the chosen intersection for the customs depot and inland port, and were not in the 2004 project cost estimates. In 2006 the Government announced a Mafraq Special Development Zone closer to the Syrian border and work on designing an inland port was abruptly suspended; in 2008 further development of the new customs depot was suspended as well, because the Army decided at that time to build a medical centre at Madounah. That plan was never carried out either. The completion report states that no development has occurred on the lands acquired at Madounah beyond the land levelling, advance works and bulk utility supply lines done in 2005 and 2006, that the customs depot has not moved from its congested site at the edge of the city, and that the Ministry of Transport and the Customs Department verbally confirmed that the depot and logistics platform might still be built there, but without any official written decision.

cases.outcome: The loans closed on 31 December 2012, three and a half years late. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group rated it Unsatisfactory, with both putting risk to development outcome at High. Land acquisition cost US$158.43 million against US$40.90 million estimated at appraisal, and total project cost came to 132 per cent over the appraisal estimate. The 500 hectares acquired at Madounah from 240 plots and 778 people remained undeveloped beyond land levelling, advance works and utility lines carried out in 2005 and 2006; neither the inland port nor the relocated customs depot had been built by the time the report was written.

cases.community: The credit paid for reconstructing the Mile 12 to Ikorodu road from four lanes to six with a bus rapid transit corridor, 13.5 kilometres of it, plus 3.55 kilometres of Akin Adesola and Wempco Roads, the Ikeja bus terminal and the Ojota bus depot. Resettlement action plans were prepared, reviewed and disclosed for the affected sites along the Mile 12 to Ikorodu and Mile 12 to Tafawa Balewa Square corridors and for the Ikeja terminal and Ojota depot. The completion report states that land acquired along the corridors and at the other sites affected 2,231 individuals and that all were compensated appropriately as planned, and its footnote breaks that down: 473 at Ikorodu, 572 at Ikorodu Market, 134 at Agric, 15 at Ogolonto, 55 at Ajegunle, 40 at Owode Section, 75 at Owode Market and 867 at Mile 12. Three groups were still unsettled when the credit closed on 31 May 2017, which is why social safeguards were rated Moderately Satisfactory. Street traders at Ikorodu roundabout were to be moved to the Oluwo Oduikan Market at Agric, built under the project, to improve traffic flow and safety around Ikorodu station. From 2016 some of them moved back to trade near the station on their own initiative; the implementing agency convened meetings in February and March 2017 with the state ministry, the local government, the Markets Board, the Markets Association, the traders and the traditional institution to agree a timeline, and the affected traders then refused to comply in May 2017. After the credit closed, Ikorodu West Council Development took over running the new market, met the stakeholders again and reached an agreement under which the traders moved into the Agric market, which is operational. A group of plantain market traders had been moved from the Mile 12 terminal site to the nearby Ajelogo market under a three-year lease. The lease expired in 2017 and they had to move again. They petitioned the World Bank in April 2017. After the credit closed, the State Ministry of Local Government and Community Affairs led a reconciliation that ended in September 2017 in an official agreement, signed by all the parties, under which the state would move them to a permanent site at Imota in Ikorodu once its construction was finished; the completion report says the traders expressed satisfaction with the final deal and pledged to work with the state to re-establish their livelihood. Eight of the people identified in the Ikeja bus terminal resettlement plan had not collected their compensation by the closing date of 31 May 2017, and all had received it by September 2017. The implementing agency's own lessons, printed in the completion report, set out what it thought had gone wrong. Resettlement plans should be holistic, sustainable and transparent to affected people, and security of land tenure is what makes them sustainable: 'Without it, the objective of the resettlement action will be defeated and another resettlement will have to occur in the future. In the case of the Ayangbunren Market traders, PAPs were displaced from one uncertain future to another equally uncertain future. In the long run, it is doubtful whether money used to secure the resettlement brings any value.' It added that terms of agreements must be properly explained, and that where affected people are illiterate or work in a language other than English an illiterate jurat should always be inserted into the agreement so that what the person signs is shown to be understood; that resettlement should not end with allocating stalls and moving people, but needs an oversight role afterwards to sort out problems and assure the resettled people's security and tenure; and that the agency should obtain long-term leases of land on which affected people are resettled, because short-term lease tenure is not ideal, and that where land cannot be acquired by government under the Land Use Act the lease should run at least ten years with a proviso letting the market associations negotiate a further lease.

cases.outcome: The credit closed on 31 May 2017 with three resettlement matters unfinished. All three were settled after closing: the Ikorodu roundabout traders moved into the Agric market, which is operational; the Mile 12 plantain traders signed an agreement in September 2017 to be moved to a permanent site at Imota in Ikorodu once its construction is complete, so at the time of the completion report they were still waiting for that site; and the eight people at the Ikeja terminal had collected their compensation by September 2017. The completion report rated the outcome Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rated it Moderately Satisfactory, on modest efficiency, 200 per cent cost overruns on the Mile 12 to Ikorodu corridor that it says cannot be fully explained by inflation and construction costs, and the cancellation of a further 27 kilometres. No document found says whether the Imota market was built or whether the plantain traders ever reached it.

The project was assessed as having high social risk. Of those, 1,289 were reviewed by committees and 61 were not yet reviewed because of the conflict that broke out in the country in December 2020; the report says those 61 would be handled by the project coordination unit and that if payment was needed the project could pay through a rural connectivity project. About 518 complaints were validated and notified to the enterprise for compensation in money or in kind. Of those 518, 429 were about houses cracking from vibration and the remaining 89 were for other damage, including trees and animals. Of the 89 complaints due financial compensation, 51 had received it, totalling FCFA 2,168,000, and 48 were still waiting for a total of FCFA 2,425,500. The report gives no figure for what the 429 house-cracking complaints received. In Cameroon, the report says all complaints received were about the loss of a piece of land to road works using machinery, and that all were processed and closed. In Chad, complaint management was handled by the project implementation unit and no complaint was received. The project reported six occupational health and safety incidents in Cameroon since the start of works, two classified as severe, two as serious and two as indicative, all accounted for through the Bank's incident reporting tool and closed, with a safeguards corrective action plan prepared and implemented; a footnote records a fatal accident in Cameroon in September 2019, for which an action plan was designed to mitigate such risks, and an incident involving an overloaded truck in the Central African Republic on 21 July 2019, classified as indicative. Two gender-based violence cases were reported to the Bank in Cameroon in September and November 2019, were handled under the project's protocol with follow-up by a specialist organisation, and were closed with disciplinary action taken under the code of conduct so that both perpetrators no longer worked for the project; in the Central African Republic a gender-based violence allegation on the Baoro-Bouar works was reported through the media, the case documentation was reviewed and the case was also closed. On safeguards, the report says performance was moderately unsatisfactory for an extended period: in Cameroon because the reforestation on the Mora-Dabanga-Kousseri section did not take place as planned in quantity or quality and because the Army Corps of Engineers did not fully comply with labour law on civilian staff; in Chad because there was no environmental and social audit to assess those aspects, and because of waste management and disposal problems on the new customs building site, for which the subcontractor agreed to remove waste from the riverside to a certified public site agreed with district authorities and to build a waterproof slab before final delivery; and in the Central African Republic because the abrupt halt to construction of the Baoro-Bouar road meant the stone quarries and borrow pits were not rehabilitated before closure.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,489 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated on any of the project's road sections. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that the completion report gives no details on whether there was land acquisition, involuntary resettlement or any issue with the physical cultural resources safeguards, while noting that the appraisal document had said road widening on the Cameroonian section would involve land acquisition along the Benoue National Park and that several tombs were to be moved.
cases.killed_note: The completion report records in a footnote that a fatal accident occurred in Cameroon in September 2019 and that an action plan was designed and was being implemented to mitigate such risks. The footnote is attached to the report's count of six occupational health and safety incidents on the project in Cameroon since the start of works, all of which the report says were accounted for through the Bank's incident reporting tool and closed, so the death was on works the credit financed: the report records that the Mora-Dabanga and Dabanga-Kousseri road works contracts in the Far North were funded under the project and that they were being carried out by the Army Corps of Engineers under the project's restructuring at the time. The report does not name the person, does not say what happened, and does not say which road section or which contractor was involved. The death was in Cameroon, not on the Baoro-Bouar section in the Central African Republic where the complaints were registered. The death is not counted in this map's figure. The rule is that a death counts only where a document gives a cause tying it to the works, and this report gives none: it records that a fatal accident occurred and not what happened. The same rule leaves ten fatalities uncounted on the Metolong dam card and three on the Nigeria erosion card, and counts three on the Serbian Corridor X card, where the completion report attributes them to unsatisfactory management of site safety.
cases.outcome: The last credits closed on 28 February 2021, eight years after the original closing date, with financing cancelled twice in the final year. On the Bank's own figures, 48 of the 89 Baoro-Bouar complaints due money were still unpaid, FCFA 2,425,500 in total, and 61 of the 1,350 complaints had not been reviewed because of the conflict that broke out in December 2020; responsibility for those 61 was left after closing to the project coordination unit, with payment if needed to come through a separate rural connectivity project. The report states in its account of what affected implementation that the Baoro-Bouar works were not completed at the time of project closure, after 34 months of work against the 20 planned, and that the abrupt halt to the construction meant the stone quarries and borrow pits were not rehabilitated before closure; its economic analysis lists the same 56 kilometre section among five road sections completed at project closing. The completion report rated the outcome Unsatisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

cases.community: The project built wastewater collection and treatment, sludge disposal, sediment removal and flood protection works in Foshan and Jiangmen. Two of the four Foshan subcomponents took land and homes. The Fenjiang River north bank comprehensive rehabilitation permanently took 85.22 mu of state-owned land and 1.68 mu of collective land, relocated 15 households with 46 people including two vulnerable people, and demolished 59,790.56 square metres of buildings, of which 2,676.39 square metres belonged to the 15 households. Fifty-three local enterprises and shops were partly affected. The resettlement plan had provided for 10 households and 38 people; the completion report gives 15 households and 46 people as the outcome. A note under the report's own comparison table says the number of relocated households changed "mainly due to family spliting after parents passed away", although the note says reduced where the table shows a rise from 10 to 15. The third phase of the Zhen'an wastewater treatment plant took 86.89 mu of state-owned land against 45 mu in the plan, because a further 41.89 mu was added for a future fourth phase of the plant, and demolished 43,324.17 square metres of enterprise buildings, of which 19,201 square metres was for that future phase; it affected 8 local enterprises, 2 owners and 16 contractors, and 256 people. Total buildings demolished rose from 105,442.04 square metres planned to 112,084.73 square metres. The count of affected people fell from 1,974 in the plan to 302, which the report attributes to no enterprise or shop being wholly relocated and to two of four vulnerable people having died. The report records some delays in carrying out resettlement actions and states that apart from those there were no other issues related to land acquisition or resettlement of affected people. It states that all assets were compensated under contracts signed before the assets were taken, at rates not lower than the plan, that the rate for demolishing the 15 private houses rose about 140 per cent, that the sampled households and enterprises received full replacement cost, and that every affected household and enterprise received 100 per cent of its compensation when the contract was signed. The external monitor reported that none of the 46 people in the 15 households changed livelihoods and that all were relocated and compensated for house demolition. The monitoring institute recorded not a single complaint or grievance during implementation. The same report gives two different counts of industrial closures in the project area and does not reconcile them: the results section says 144 industrial enterprises were shut down or relocated during the project period, and an annex says 34 enterprises were closed or relocated out of the Foshan urban area. Both figures describe municipal pollution-control action rather than works the loan financed.

cases.community: The project built water treatment plants and distribution networks, wastewater collection networks and treatment plants, storm water networks, associated roads, river embankment works and the Qingshankejiawu landfill at Meicheng town in Jiande, across eight counties and districts and 24 towns, townships and communities in four municipalities of Zhejiang. The completion report's resettlement annex gives the outcome against the plan. Permanent land acquisition came to 98.73 hectares and affected 513 households and 1,731 people, against 611 households and 2,084 people planned. Houses were demolished over 26,606 square metres, affecting 73 households and 281 people, against 203 households and 730 people planned, a drop of 47 per cent in area which the report attributes to a revised utility design in Tonglu and to a dropped civil works contract in Pan'an. Temporary land use came to 95.89 hectares and affected 789 households and 2,827 people. The largest house demolition was at Meicheng in Jiande, 35 households and 145 people, where the landfill was built; the report lists among the project's resettlement experiences the protection of households in the buffer zone of the landfill and the wastewater treatment plant in Jiande by relocating and resettling them. Demolition also took place at Jiande, 14 households and 46 people, Shenze in Jinhua, 3 households and 9 people, Qujiang, 1 household and 5 people, and Longyou, 20 households and 76 people. Relocation increased in Jiande and Qujiang because households in the buffer zones of the landfill and the Qujiang wastewater treatment plant were added, and in Longyou because urban planning changed to fit the expanding urban area. The total number of people affected by land acquisition and resettlement was 4,839, 14 per cent fewer than planned. The final resettlement cost was RMB 142 million, about US$20.88 million, 15.5 per cent below the plan's budget. The report states that compensation standards for land acquisition and house demolition were not lower than those in the plans, that all compensation was paid before relocation and before the impacts occurred, that all 1,207 eligible affected people were identified and placed in the national social security programme, and that the external monitor and Bank supervision found the affected people had restored their standard of living and were generally satisfied. At Qujiang the project acquired the affected houses but let the households stay until the last moment before demolition.

Its project management office and project implementation units ran the works and the grievance mechanism (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 22 June 2020).

cases.community: The project was named for the water environment but what it built was flood control and urban drainage: embankment and river works on the Hongshui and Beizhijiang rivers and the Caoxiegou stream, and sewage and storm drainage networks in the old urban area of Laibin city. It acquired 48.02 hectares of land, 15.35 hectares state-owned and 32.67 hectares collectively owned rural land, about 64 per cent of it cultivated. Acquiring the state-owned land affected 11 enterprises and demolished 63,953 square metres of structures, the great majority of them vacant workshops. The land acquisition in the rural areas economically displaced 215 households with 1,075 people and physically displaced 416 families with 2,363 people, demolishing 87,500 square metres of residential housing. The resettlement action plan had provided for the demolition of 36,097.3 square metres of rural residential houses affecting 93 households and 339 people. The outcome was therefore about four and a half times the planned number of households and seven times the planned number of people, and about 2.4 times the planned area of housing. Planned permanent land acquisition was 359.31 mu and the actual figure was 720.35 mu. The actual resettlement cost was RMB 172.66 million, about US$24.88 million, more than three times the appraisal estimate of RMB 54.65 million; the completion report attributes that partly to the increased volume and partly to new local compensation standards set in 2017 for land acquisition, building replacement cost and other compensation. The report states that resettlement funds were paid to affected people on time from the annual fiscal budget, that affected land and property were surveyed and valued with the effective participation of the affected people, that the project gave replacement apartments with tenure security instead of cash compensation, and that vocational training, small credit and social pensions were provided. It records that no complaint was logged through the grievance mechanism during implementation and that there were no outstanding grievances at closing, and says the affected people did not use the mechanism because land acquisition and resettlement issues were resolved through public participation and consultation. The external monitoring agency concluded that the land acquisition and relocation were legally completed and that the objectives of the resettlement plans were materially achieved. The completion report's own lesson from the project is to estimate land and resettlement complexity and cost realistically in rapidly urbanising areas, noting that the costs here were more than three times the appraisal estimate.
