Updating the environmental and social impact assessment and the resettlement action plan took about four years and the Mozambican government approved them in April 2018, seven and a half years after the project became effective; the Bank took a further six months to approve the plan. Safeguards performance was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory again and again during those four years. Once the plan was approved, land acquisition and the financing of the houses moved quickly, but the parts of the plan the government was responsible for did not, for lack of capacity and budget. The dedicated consultant and service provider needed to carry out the resettlement were recruited only in December 2019 and February 2020, five months and three months before the project was due to close. In the meantime many of the newly built houses stood empty and were vandalised, with doors, locks and window fixtures stolen, so that on-site security was needed. The Bank's supervision missions in March and June 2018 called for caution in starting civil works because most of the households still to be resettled were living in the works area. The project closed on 30 June 2020 with parts of the resettlement plan and the livelihood restoration plan unfinished: auxiliary structures such as outside kitchens and barns, some compensation for commercial stalls, garages and warehouses, the relocation of existing gravesites, the issue of land and property titles, agricultural extension services, and the social and environmental audits. The government was responsible for land acquisition and for paying cash allowances and compensation, but by the time the plan began to be implemented the country had entered a fiscal crisis that severely limited the funds. The option of having the project itself pay the cash compensation was considered in 2017 and not pursued. Resettlement kits of farming and household tools were sourced from other government agencies and distributed, as were maize and bean seed. One worker was killed during construction in a vehicle accident the report calls preventable, whose root cause it puts mainly on the lack of senior management commitment in the contractor's organisation and to some extent on the borrower's inadequate capacity to manage safeguards. Occupational health and safety performance was poor at first and was corrected later through penalties, training and monitoring. Work stopped altogether on several occasions, including a five-week suspension in 2019 for non-compliance with health and safety requirements, intermittent labour stoppages and tensions in the local community, and a two-month hold on the saddle dam while unexploded ordnance found in the area was cleared.
cases.displaced_label: project-affected people resettled, from the World Bank completion report
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 935 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's own count of people resettled is 660, into 133 houses at four sites. Delays in the census and socio-economic surveys made the number of affected people hard to settle, because each update recorded new families settling in the dam surroundings.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2020 with the resettlement plan and the livelihood restoration plan both unfinished and with some compensation and allowances unpaid. The Mozambican government was to finish and pay for the outstanding work with support from the panel of experts and the Bank, and the ministry later mobilised internal budget resources for it. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that it was not clear how committed the government was to financing and completing the pending activities. A grievance mechanism remained active in the dam area and in the four resettlement villages.

cases.confidence_note: The resettlement count, the unfinished compensation, the vandalised houses and the worker's death all come from the Bank's own completion report, and the unfinished compensation is confirmed by the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of the Corumana resettlement was found. Two of the completion report's statements of fact are footnoted to personal communications with named Bank staff rather than to documents, and nothing here rests on those: the vandalism of the houses is footnoted to a personal communication of 4 February 2021, and the decision not to have the project fund cash compensation to one of 12 February 2021. The 660 resettled people, the 133 houses, the list of pending activities and the fatality are all in the report's own text. No document found names an affected household, says how many households the 660 people made up, or quantifies what compensation was still unpaid at closing. The review's safeguards section quotes the completion report's paragraph on occupational health and safety but omits the sentence about the fatality that follows it. The review carries no date anywhere on the page; the date used here is the Bank's own document date from its archive, unverified at document level.
cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A, full assessment, and triggered the policies on environmental assessment, natural habitats, safety of dams, involuntary resettlement and projects on international waterways. An environmental and social impact assessment, a social impact assessment, an environmental management plan and a resettlement action plan were prepared for the completion of the dam and disclosed in country and through the Bank's InfoShop. An environmental and social service provider was hired to review and update the assessment and the plan, both originally completed in 2011, to take account of new and more demanding Mozambican regulations on resettlement and economic impact assessment; that work took four years. The project design included a standalone component for safeguards compliance. Under the international waterways policy the government formally notified South Africa and Swaziland during preparation under the revised SADC protocol and the interim IncoMaputo agreement, and complied with South Africa's request for constant feedback through the Tripartite Permanent Technical Committee. Under the natural habitats policy, environmental flow requirements and water quality monitoring were built into the dam's operating management system, with base flow and freshet releases and a requirement to hold the dam below 117 metres above sea level except in severe floods, to limit backwater effects in the Sabie Game Reserve and Kruger National Park in South Africa. An emergency preparedness plan was prepared under the dam safety policy. The borrower was recommended to commission an independent environmental audit after the fatality; that audit found the contractor's environmental management partially compliant (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 20 May 2021; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 3 November 2021).

cases.title: Three Line Workers Killed and Compensation Paid Late on the Ethiopia-Sudan Interconnector
cases.place: The Bahir Dar to Gondar, Gondar to Shehedi and Shehedi to Metema transmission line, Amhara region, Ethiopia, to the Sudanese border at Gallabat
cases.point: Bahir Dar, the southern end of the line and the start of the Bahir Dar to Gondar section where construction began before the affected people had been paid (OpenStreetMap city point for Bahir Dar)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-43750 of SDR 26.44 million for the Ethiopia-Sudan Interconnector under the Nile Basin Initiative (P074011), approved 20 December 2007 and effective 31 July 2008, with SDR 24.37 million disbursed. Original closing was 31 December 2011 and actual closing 30 June 2013, after restructurings on 16 December 2011 and 14 June 2012. Environmental category B. The whole of the Bank's financing was coded to transmission and distribution of electricity. The implementing agencies were the Ministry of Water and Energy and the Ethiopian Electric Power Corporation. The completion report of 23 December 2013 rated outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Moderately Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Low; the Independent Evaluation Group's review posted 29 July 2014 agreed on outcome and gave risk to development outcome as Negligible to Low. Financial management was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory for most of implementation (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR2925, 23 December 2013; IEG ICR Review, posted 29 July 2014).

companies.name: Energoinvest
companies.role: The subcontractor for the transmission line. It prepared the environmental, health and safety plan for the line works. The completion report records that over the course of construction three deaths and 11 accidents occurred, that the subcontractor neglected to require its personnel to use safety equipment such as safety belts and helmets, which contributed to the injuries, and that the inappropriate erection of two towers contributed to two tower collapses in 2010 that caused nine of the 11 accidents. The report records that the transmission line contractor paid compensation to the affected families and that the Bank team confirmed the payments were completed (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 December 2013).

companies.name: Ethiopian Electric Power Corporation (EEPCo)
companies.role: The Ethiopian state electricity utility, which was the project's implementing agency. It discussed safety practices with the subcontractor after the deaths and asked it to follow compensation procedures; it also paid ETB 25.11 million in compensation to project-affected people, and allowed the supervision engineer's contract to expire before the works were finished, so that supervision by environmental and social experts ended earlier than planned (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 December 2013).

cases.community: Despite the project's name, which carries the Nile Basin Initiative, the works were a high-voltage power link: 296.5 km of transmission line and the upgrading of three substations, running from Bahir Dar through Gondar and Shehedi to Metema on the Sudanese border, opposite Gallabat. The line involved expanding the existing 260 km single-circuit 230 kV line from Bahir Dar to Shehedi by building a second single-circuit system from Bahir Dar to Gondar and a second line on the existing double-circuit towers between Gondar and Shehedi, plus a new 36.5 km double-circuit 230/220 kV line from Shehedi to Metema. Three deaths and 11 accidents occurred during construction of the line. One worker was killed in June 2010 through negligence, having used no scaffolding or care when crossing a road to string a line. Two more were killed in 2011 in an accident during the erection of a tower, having not worn safety belts. Nine of the 11 accidents came from two tower collapses in 2010 caused by towers being put up wrongly. The completion report states that the Bank team requested and received information on the compensation paid to the families of the dead. On the resettlement side, construction work started on the Bahir Dar to Gondar section before the affected people had received their compensation; the utility had to be told so that the construction schedule could be changed to pay first, and three of the woredas, the district administrations, delayed their payments, which held up completion of that line by eight months. Of the 4,490 affected people, five families were paid compensation for damage to their property but received no land, because they held no legal ownership title from the local government and Ethiopian law makes title a condition of land compensation. Three of those five families refused to move and went to court for redress. They lost their appeals. The Bank recommended that the utility arrange special assistance for their relocation anyway, the utility asked the districts to consider it, and the completion report states that the families have been successfully relocated since the project closed. In total ETB 25.11 million, about US$1.39 million, was paid in compensation to 4,490 affected people.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,415 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts 4,490 affected people paid compensation. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated, except the five families denied land compensation, of whom three refused to move and were relocated after the project closed.
cases.suppression: Three of the five families who were paid for damage to their property but given no land refused to move and sought redress in the courts. They lost their appeals, and the completion report states they were relocated after the project closed.
cases.outcome: The credit closed on 30 June 2013 after an 18-month extension, with the line sections completed in August 2010 and 2011 and the substations late. The completion report records the environmental management plan and the resettlement action plan as implemented by closing. The three families who had refused to move were relocated after the project closed, with special assistance the Bank recommended after they had lost in court.

cases.confidence_note: The deaths, the accidents, their causes, the construction that began before compensation was paid and the five families denied land compensation all come from the Bank's own completion report; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report repeats the same account of the deaths almost word for word. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of these deaths or of this line's land acquisition was found. Both documents record the compensation as late. The completion report says work began on the Bahir Dar to Gondar section before the affected people were paid and that three woredas delayed payments, costing eight months; the review's section on administrative efficiency says outstanding compensation owed by the district administrations caused delays and rescheduling of work, with an overall delay of eight months, and its section on government performance lists ensuring that compensation payments were timely among the things a higher level of government input could have achieved. The documents give no names, no dates for the five families' court cases, no date for their relocation and no figure for what the three woredas owed. The three deaths are counted here because the report names their causes: negligence in crossing a road to string a line, and personnel not wearing safety belts during a tower erection, after a subcontractor that did not require safety equipment to be used. The report does not say whether the dead were employees of the subcontractor or of anyone else. The amount paid to the families of the dead is not given in any document found.
cases.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered the policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. An environmental and social impact assessment containing an environmental management plan, with resettlement action plans for Ethiopia and for Sudan, was prepared with support from the Eastern Nile Technical Regional Office of the Nile Basin Initiative, and the Bank disclosed the management plan and the two plans in the two countries in 2007. Monitoring of safeguards was to be done by the supervision engineer, with auditing and implementation by the Ethiopian Electric Power Corporation and independent monitoring and oversight by the regional office, which also served as the Bank team's route for information on the Sudanese portion. Implementation of both plans was completed by closing, with adjustments to synchronise the resettlement plan with the revised construction timetable. The utility let the supervision engineer's contract expire before the facilities were finished rather than extend it as the Bank team suggested, so supervision by environmental and social experts ended earlier than planned, and a restructuring of the utility's environment management unit during implementation further weakened its monitoring. Ethiopian law makes a legal ownership title issued by the local government a condition of land compensation, which is why five families who lost property received cash but no land (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 December 2013).

cases.title: Two Years Without Water or Power in the Gameleira Resettlement Village, Ceara
cases.place: Gameleira dam agrovila, on the rural boundary of Itapipoca, Trairi and Tururu, Ceara, Brazil, and the Umari and Jenipapeiro dam resettlements at Madalena and Baixio
cases.point: Itapipoca, the municipality the Bank's completion report gives for the Gameleira dam; Agencia Publica places the dam on the boundary of the rural areas of Trairi, Itapipoca and Tururu, about 150 km from Fortaleza (OpenStreetMap administrative point for Itapipoca)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-76300 of US$103.0 million, the additional financing to the Ceara Integrated Water Resources Management Project, PROGERIRH (P110487), for the same objectives as the original loan IBRD-45310 for P006449. The completion report's data sheet gives approval on 18 December 2008 and its text says the Board approved it on 17 December 2008; it was signed only in September 2009 and became effective in November 2009, with a closing date of December 2011, leaving an effective two-year implementation period. US$98.33 million of the additional loan was disbursed. Delays in signing came from the procedures for processing loans between the federal government and the state and the need for Senate approval. Across both phases the original commitment was US$136 million and US$237.28 million was disbursed. Environmental category A. The implementing agency was the state Secretariat of Water Resources, with the water company COGERH and the works superintendence SOHIDRA executing parts of it. The completion report of 28 December 2012 rated outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and downgraded overall safeguard compliance to Moderately Unsatisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review posted 21 June 2013 agreed on outcome, put risk to development outcome at High against the report's Moderate, and rated Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory against the report's Moderately Satisfactory (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2012; IEG ICR Review, posted 21 June 2013).

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD), first phase
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-45310 for the original Ceara Integrated Water Resources Management Project (P006449), approved 6 January 2000 and effective 24 May 2000, which built the first six dams. The additional financing built five more (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2012).

companies.name: EIT
companies.role: The contractor on the Gameleira dam and agrovila works, named by Agencia Publica, which reports that the firm entered judicial recovery during construction and could not complete the works, that the state secretariat suspended payments to it in August 2011 by court order and that the works stopped in December 2011, by which time families had been living in the agrovila since January of that year. A state audit prosecutor's representation of March 2012 was filed against the secretariat and against EIT (Agencia Publica, 16 April 2015).

companies.name: Secretaria dos Recursos Hidricos do Ceara (SRH)
companies.role: The water resources secretariat of the state government of Ceara, the project's main implementing agency. It maintained special units to manage resettlement and the environment and to coordinate environmental mitigation and compensation. The completion report rates its performance under the additional financing Moderately Unsatisfactory, citing insufficient action on construction delays and inadequate attention to resettlement and environmental mitigation works, and says its supervision capacity was not strong enough in the later years (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2012).

companies.name: Superintendencia de Obras Hidraulicas (SOHIDRA)
companies.role: The state works superintendence of Ceara, responsible for surveillance of contractors' performance. The state government decided to stop using an external supervision firm, against an agreement with the Bank that external supervision would run throughout implementation, and to supervise through SOHIDRA instead; the completion report states that SOHIDRA was not adequately staffed or trained to supervise environmental and social aspects of the contractors' work, and that this affected the quality of supervision of the works and the environmental mitigation activities (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2012).

cases.community: Across the two phases the project built 11 dams and affected 2,174 families: 1,394 under the first phase's six dams and 780 under the additional financing's five, at Gameleira in Itapipoca, Umari in Madalena, Jatoba in Ipueiras, Jenipapeiro in Baixio and Mamoeiro in Antonina do Norte. The completion report's resettlement table sets out what each family received. Of the 2,174, 261 families took houses in new agricultural villages, the agrovilas, with infrastructure and a farm plot; 377 were resettled on unaffected parts of their own farms; 491 bought new homes themselves with a resettlement grant; and 12 bought homes in nearby towns, making 1,141 families moved. The remaining 1,033 were landowners who took cash compensation, for whom the report records no move. Under the additional financing alone 140 families went into agrovilas and 185 to remaining areas, 87 resettled themselves and 368 took cash. The families resettled into the Gameleira agrovila in January 2011 had no water or electricity supply until December 2012, nearly two years, despite repeated recommendations and alerts from the Bank's supervision missions in 2011 and 2012. By December 2012 the handover of their farm plots was still unfinished because the demarcation was incomplete, and neither the land titles nor the fencing of the agrovila had been resolved. The completion report states that the titling of lots had not been done in any of the agrovilas the project financed under either phase. At Jenipapeiro the dam was filled in 2011 before the power line running through the reservoir basin had been moved, which left the families settled in the agrovila without power and therefore without water, because their supply depended on electric pumps; the problem was solved in early 2012 after intense effort by Bank missions. At Umari the 35 houses the project built in 2011 developed structural problems and had to be demolished and rebuilt, which the original contractor did at no extra cost in groups of five houses while the families were moved temporarily into houses rented by the government; the completion report says this poor construction quality should have been identified during the works and was being resolved only in December 2012, more than a year after they were finished. Fourteen compensation cases were still open at December 2012, all of them landowners who had taken cash and were still disputing the valuation of their land; most had had 80 per cent of the amount deposited as a court bond. Agencia Publica reported on the Gameleira agrovila in April 2015. It gives the dam's cost as R$40 million, R$18 million of it World Bank money, and 180 families affected according to the state secretariat, 91 of them living on the site and losing part or all of their land. It records that EIT entered judicial recovery during construction of the agrovila and could not finish the works. It reports one resident receiving R$7,000 in indemnity and another saying each house was paid R$5,000, against a secretariat ceiling of R$12,000 for owners who lost more than two-thirds of their land. It found the agrovila's only water source to be a well with a desalination unit treating about a quarter of the water used each day, giving each family 36 litres a day for drinking and cooking and leaving the salty well water for everything else; the pipeline that was the original plan, for a minimum capacity of 30,000 litres, had never been built, and although a contract of about R$250,000 had been awarded to another firm, I. C. Projetos e Construcoes, the work had not started. Power arrived only in late 2012, after the electricity company Coelce cut an illegal connection in January 2012. The health post was an empty concrete shell and the refuse collection and leisure areas were never delivered. The association president Paulo Sergio de Moraes Alves told the reporters that people there had to go on using the salty water, and that a water tanker could take days to arrive. A resident, Maria Socorro, said they had not been compensated but humoured into leaving. In March 2012 a state prosecutor at the state audit court filed a representation describing the families' conditions as sub-human. The Bank told the reporters that its missions had found the water supply adequate. The same report gives figures for the first phase's Aracoiaba dam, finished in December 2002 at about R$14 million, which affected 608 families, 333 of them living on the site, and also faced low compensation and incomplete agrovilas, and says that World Bank-financed works in Ceara affected at least 4,625 families according to the state secretariat.
cases.displaced_label: families moved under the four resettlement options in the World Bank completion report's resettlement table (261 into agrovilas, 377 onto remaining parts of their own farms, 491 self-resettled, 12 into towns); 412 of them under this additional financing
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,176 for this additional financing, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's resettlement table counts families, not people: 780 families affected under the additional financing's five dams and 1,394 under the first phase's six, 2,174 in all. Of those 2,174, the table's own columns give 261 resettled into agrovilas, 377 onto unaffected parts of their own farms, 491 self-resettled with a grant and 12 into homes in towns, which is 1,141 families moved; the other 1,033 were landowners who took cash compensation and whose movement the report does not record. Under the additional financing alone the four relocation options come to 412 families of 780. Agencia Publica gives 180 families affected at Gameleira on the state secretariat's figures, 91 of them living on the site, which matches the completion report's total of 180 for that dam.
cases.outcome: The additional financing closed in December 2012 with two of its five dams complete and three still under construction, at 75 per cent for Gameleira, 92 per cent for Mamoeiro and 96 per cent for Jatoba, and with all six of its planned conveyance pipelines unfinished. The Ipaumirim pipeline works were halted by a judicial dispute between the contractor and the implementing agency. The Bank said it would keep supervising the pending works and resettlement activities into 2013. Overall safeguard compliance was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review found the state had departed from the procedures agreed with the Bank and so was not in compliance with the resettlement policy, particularly on the timely payment of fair compensation to those displaced, with long delays in issuing land titles for agrovila residents. The review records that many resettlement issues, especially titling and compensation, remained outstanding. By April 2015 Agencia Publica found the Gameleira agrovila still without the pipeline that had been planned and still drinking desalinated well water.

cases.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered the policies on environmental assessment, natural habitats, pest management, physical cultural resources, involuntary resettlement and dam safety. A regional environmental assessment covering five river basins was carried out during preparation of the original project, and environmental assessments and management plans for the large hydraulic works were approved by the Bank before appraisal in 1999 and before approval of the additional financing in 2008. Bank review and approval were required for any proposed reservoir, each of which needed an acceptable resettlement plan and an environmental impact assessment and management plan. Works contracts had to oblige the contractor to clear vegetation in the inundation area and to mark or fence the permanent protection strip on the reservoir margin, and an environmental construction manual was produced to guide supervision. Supervision of the works by private consultant firms was to cover the contractors' compliance with the safeguards and the management plans; the state government discontinued that external supervision during the additional financing, against its agreement with the Bank. Every family was to be offered a choice between resettling itself with a grant and being resettled in an agrovila with a farm plot. Brazil has no resettlement law, and the completion report calls the secretariat's effort to carry out resettlement to Bank rules within the Brazilian legal framework commendable. Dam interventions were evaluated by a safety panel set up for the purpose (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2012; IEG ICR Review, posted 21 June 2013).

cases.title: Riverbank Dwellers Moved Late and Three Workers Killed on the Ganga Clean-up
cases.place: The Patna riverfront development on the Ganga, including Bhairwa Ghat and the Digha sewage treatment plant site, and the Beur and Begusarai works, Bihar, India
cases.point: Patna, where the riverfront development was the only project investment requiring full land acquisition, affecting 249 families, and where the Digha and Beur sites lie (OpenStreetMap city point for Patna)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA and IBRD)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-49550 of US$199 million and loan IBRD-80650 of US$801 million for the National Ganga River Basin Project (P119085), approved 31 May 2011 and effective 18 August 2011. The IBRD loan was cut to US$334,825,259 and US$514,233,533 was disbursed in all against the original US$1 billion commitment. Original closing was 31 December 2019 and actual closing 30 December 2021. Total project cost fell from US$1.556 billion to US$673,583,533. Environmental category A, full assessment. The implementing agency was the National Mission for Clean Ganga in the Ministry of Jal Shakti. The project financing agreement was revised to include the provisions of India's Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013. Safeguards performance at closing was rated Moderately Satisfactory. The completion report of 28 February 2023 rated outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation quality Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review agreed on all three (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2023; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 29 June 2023).

companies.name: National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG)
companies.role: The mission under the Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation in India's Ministry of Jal Shakti that implemented the project, working through state programme management groups. The completion report records that the programme management groups had dedicated systems for safeguards implementation, and that procurement capacity at state level and at the Central Pollution Control Board remained low (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2023).

cases.community: The project financed sewage treatment plants, sewer networks and a riverfront development to cut pollution going into the Ganga. Most investments used land already under existing treatment plants or government land transferred after a no-objection certificate, and where private land was needed the project bought it directly; the completion report records that direct purchase was dogged by prolonged price negotiations, contested ownership rights and complications in paying the final amounts. The only investment that required full land acquisition was the Patna riverfront development, which affected 249 families. Those affected were encroachers living in shacks and mud houses on the riverbank. Because compensation against the existing value of their assets and income would have been negligible, a flat rate of INR 150,000 and land for a house were agreed instead. The land allotment was then stalled for two years, and in the end extra cash was given instead of land. The completion report records a further complication: the sites were handed over to the contractor before the affected people had been resettled and before compensation was paid. The affected people were tracked down and compensated, and the report says this affected implementation of the investment, especially at Bhairwa Ghat. Beyond the riverfront, 20 households were affected by partial land acquisition and 234 households by economic losses. At closing all resettlement action plans had been fully implemented and one abbreviated plan was still open, to compensate three affected people at the Digha sewage treatment plant site. All the riverfront families were eventually compensated and given training to restore their incomes. In 2021 two fatal incidents at project sites in Bihar killed three labourers, one at Begusarai in March and two at Beur in May. The completion report's annex on the project's history states that the root-cause analysis indicated the accidents occurred through negligence on occupational health and safety training of workers and supervisors; its safeguards section says the root-cause analysis of both incidents pointed at gaps in site management and occupational health and safety practice, and the Bank's own supervision records had reported unsatisfactory performance on those points across the whole implementation period of the works component. After the deaths the incident reporting procedures were followed, the next of kin were compensated, a safety audit was carried out and regular on-site briefings were held. The completion report states that three workers died under circumstances that appear to have been preventable, and that site management and worker safety remained a perennial concern from the start of the works component, with the outcome proving unsatisfactory in Begusarai and Beur. On procurement, Bank guidelines were violated and misprocurement was declared on the Buxar sewage treatment plant and sewerage works, confidential information was leaked during the bid evaluation for the Munger sewage treatment plant and sewerage network, and preliminary bid evaluation reports prepared by implementing agencies were contested by the mission and the Bank and had to be revised. All three instances were in Bihar.
cases.displaced_label: project-affected families on the Patna riverfront, from the World Bank completion report; the report calls them project affected families and does not separately count those physically moved

cases.community: The project treated gully erosion and watershed sites, beginning in seven states, Anambra, Abia, Cross River, Ebonyi, Edo, Enugu and Imo, and scaling up to 23. It supported communities inside treated sites either by compensating them for lost productive assets and activities, through 83 resettlement action plans that the completion report says benefited 9,471 affected people, or through livelihood activities. By 31 October 2022 the project had compensated 9,696 affected people and fully implemented 94 resettlement action plans over its ten years. At closing 21 of the 23 states had fully implemented their plans. Two states, Abia and Imo, could not locate 32 affected people, and an escrow account was opened and funded with counterpart money to pay them if they came forward. Imo State was still implementing its resettlement plan at closing, with the compensation money held in an escrow account. Unfinished civil works remained in three states, which the completion report says could lead to the destruction of properties, the displacement of people or public risk; every affected state except Imo prepared and carried out an exit plan with measures including cordoning off the unfinished sites with signs, telling the people who would have benefited about the risk, and securing a binding commitment from the state to finish the works. Imo State provided no letter of comfort for its unfinished sites. Over the project's life more than 1,160 complaints were received across the 23 states and all were recorded as resolved. Three workers died at project sites. The report records the deaths as occupational health and safety fatalities, each of which triggered the Bank's environmental and social incident response procedure, and says the root-cause analyses found them not systemic but one-off cases; it gives no cause for any of the three. The report's economic analysis, in valuing the displacement the works avoided, uses a figure of 5,721 project-affected people actually displaced by the project, drawn from resettlement plan implementation reports at 84 sites, and then extrapolates to 7,015 while referring to 81 sites. Sub-grants for livelihood activities such as waste management, livestock farming, plant nurseries, gabion box welding and block moulding reached 35,977 beneficiaries by closing, of whom the report gives 15,977 as male and 20,509 as female, figures that come to 36,486 rather than 35,977.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,087 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated in the project's safeguards reporting. The same bullet then extrapolates to 7,015 people while switching from 84 project sites to 81, without explaining either the new total or the change in sites, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review, which rates the quality of the completion report Modest, does not carry 5,721 or 7,015 at all. A number used as an input to a benefit calculation is not the document's count of people displaced, so it is not entered here. The counts the report gives in its social safeguards section are 9,696 affected people compensated as of 31 October 2022 under 94 resettlement action plans fully implemented, and 9,471 affected people benefiting from 83 plans.
cases.killed_note: Three workers died at project sites. The World Bank's completion report of 19 July 2023 records them in its environmental safeguards section as occupational health and safety fatalities that triggered the Bank's environmental and social incident response procedure, and says the root-cause analyses found they were not systemic issues but one-off cases. The report gives no cause, no date, no place and no identity for any of the three, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the same account without adding any. They are therefore not counted.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2022 after a two-year extension. Twenty-one of 23 states had fully implemented their resettlement plans; Imo State had not, and its compensation money was left in an escrow account, as was the money for the 32 people Abia and Imo could not find. Civil works were unfinished in three states, with the state governments committed to completing them as part of the borrower's responsibility. The completion report's own recommendation was to focus counterpart funding on compensating affected people in each state.

cases.community: The project upgraded and rehabilitated existing rural roads, tracks and trails in 20 districts and then 10 more. The roads were built largely on land the communities gave up. The completion report states that the community donated 2.13 million square metres of land, which at prevailing market rates it estimates at NPR 5.63 billion, about US$56.3 million, and that this is several times more than the NPR 64.4 million, about US$0.65 million, that the project provided as assistance to the affected people. The report presents this as a noteworthy feature of community involvement. It also records that implementation of the social safeguard requirements was so slow at first that at the mid-term review in November 2008 it was rated highly unsatisfactory, among other things because of non-payment of compensation to severely project affected families, there being no resettlement action plan as required. In response the project coordination unit assessed the impacts of the voluntary land donation and the numbers of affected families and prepared a remedial action plan, whose implementation resolved 97 per cent of the land ownership issues by the end of the project. The remaining owners could not be compensated: they were either absentee landowners or their land was in litigation. In total there were 12,558 affected families, of which 204 severely affected families, 162 for land, 37 for structures and 5 for loss of livelihood, had received their assistance by the end of the project. The Independent Evaluation Group's review, summarising page 8 of the report, states that the report also gives 11,460 of 11,866 landowners as compensated; at that point in the published completion report the figures sit inside a parenthesis that is blank in the document's text, so the review's summary is the only place the pair can be read. The report's borrower annex records that the project awarded a letter of appreciation to all 11,866 land donors and displayed their names in public places. Those who donated more than 10 per cent of their holding were compensated for the part above 10 per cent. Transfer of donated land titles was completed for 97.1 per cent under the additional financing, which the borrower's own report attributes to landowners being unavailable and to a few disputed cases. The Independent Evaluation Group's review calls the completion report's treatment of the resettlement policy confusing on four counts: it is unclear how far the Bank scrutinised the voluntary land donation process, which the review says can lead to abuse through forceful land acquisition; the report says there were 12,558 affected families of which only the 204 severely affected received compensation, then says 11,460 of 11,866 landowners were compensated, without stating whether those totals include the donors and the severely affected families; it is unknown how many people were actually compensated during implementation or whether the compensation was adequate; and the report is inconsistent in its rating of social safeguards, giving Satisfactory in one paragraph and Moderately Satisfactory in another. The review's own lesson is that voluntary donation of land transfers for project activities may lead to abuse, and that careful monitoring by the Bank can help ensure that abuse does not occur and that the donation is genuinely voluntary. The borrower's own section of the completion report says that all the roads upgraded under the additional financing were existing roads and caused minimum negative social impact, and that the project did not displace a single individual. Environmental safeguards were a concern until late 2012 because of delays in preparing the initial environmental examinations and management plans, in designing site-specific mitigation works and in carrying them out; performance varied from road to road between moderately unsatisfactory and moderately satisfactory.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,028 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 12,558 affected families, 11,866 land donors and 204 severely affected families. The borrower's own section of the same report states that the project did not displace a single individual, and no Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2013 after a three-year extension. Social safeguards ended with a rating the completion report gives twice and differently, as Satisfactory in one paragraph and Moderately Satisfactory in another, after a highly unsatisfactory rating at mid-term for non-payment of compensation. Ninety-seven per cent of land ownership issues were resolved; the rest were absentee owners or land in litigation. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that it is unknown how many people were actually compensated during implementation or whether the compensation was adequate.

companies.name: Office National de l'Eau et de l'Assainissement (ONEA)
companies.role: Burkina Faso's national water and sanitation utility, a state-owned company, which implemented the project and whose environmental and social unit was responsible for the safeguard instruments. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that it started the Ouagadougou water transmission civil works funded under the additional financing without preparing a resettlement action plan and without compensating four project-affected people, which brought the works to a halt. cases.community: The project extended water production, storage and distribution and sanitation in Ouagadougou, Bobo-Dioulasso and three other urban centres. Six original subprojects required compensation payments to landowners: secondary water distribution networks in Bobo-Dioulasso, Dedougou and Koudougou, boreholes in Bobo-Dioulasso and Dedougou, and a distribution line in Koudougou. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that no physical settlement occurred because of those six. Under the additional financing the utility began the Ouagadougou water transmission civil works without preparing a resettlement action plan and without compensating four project-affected people, which breaches the Bank's resettlement policy. The Bank was informed in December 2016 and the works were suspended on 15 December 2016. The Bank and the utility agreed an action plan to bring the project back into compliance, the utility prepared a resettlement plan, the Bank approved it in April 2017, and the suspension of the civil works was lifted in June 2017. The two documents count the people left unpaid at different moments and do not agree on how many there were in all. The review states that, excluding 49 project-affected people who could not be located, all the other 768 were compensated by May 2017, and that the compensation amounts for the 49 were deposited in an escrow account for future payment, which makes 817 people. The completion report, written at closing in December 2020, states that some affected people remained unfound despite three reminders from the project and could not be compensated, giving 26 of 756 affected people on lot 2.2 and 4 of 79 on lot 6.1, which is 30 of 835, and that the utility opened an escrow account holding their compensation in case they came forward. The number unpaid is therefore lower at closing than in May 2017, while the number of affected people is 18 higher, and neither document explains either figure or says which lots the review's 817 covers. The completion report also records that where works started late the utility faced complaints from people trying to settle on the land after it had been secured, and that its social and environmental specialists stressed the importance of keeping records so that evidence of compensation and of eligibility would not be missing.
cases.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,953 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that no physical settlement occurred because of the six original subprojects that required compensation, and counts 817 project-affected people on the additional financing's Ouagadougou works, of whom 768 were compensated by May 2017; the completion report's two lots on the same works come to 835 affected people, of whom 30 were never compensated. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
cases.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2019 with a Satisfactory safeguards rating. The suspension of the Ouagadougou civil works was lifted in June 2017 once a resettlement plan had been written and approved and the people who could be found had been paid. The compensation for those who could not be found, 49 people by the Independent Evaluation Group's count or 30 by the completion report's, was left in an escrow account to be paid if they came forward.

lenders_add.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders_add.role: The Kenya Transport Sector Support Project (P124109) closed on 31 December 2020. The completion report of 29 January 2021 rated social safeguards performance Moderately Unsatisfactory at close and listed four areas of non-compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy: the original engineering design for the interchanges was not based on minimising resettlement, so design updates during implementation disrupted the resettlement action plans and produced many resettlement complaints; the road corridors were not clear and free of encumbrances and compensation of affected people was not completed before the works began; carrying out the resettlement plans was lengthy and delayed, because of the design updates and insufficient government counterpart budget for compensation; and there was no well-funded, systematic stakeholder engagement or grievance process at the start. Environmental assessment was downgraded from Satisfactory to Moderately Satisfactory in November 2018 over poor management of quarry and borrow sites, health and safety risks and incidents at construction sites, community complaints about drainage and lack of access to residential homes, and the Inspection Panel case on the Webuye interchange; the rating was retained at Moderately Satisfactory in December 2019. The completion report records that on the major road contracts contractors mobilised before affected people had been compensated for land, property or business, so contractors could not take full possession of the sites, which slowed the works and had the Government paying for idle equipment and staff, and that this happened even though the safeguard instruments had been finalised well before the works began. At the time the report was written, rehabilitation of materials sites and compensation of affected people were still continuing, and the Bank told the Government it would remain engaged until all safeguards activities were complete (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 29 January 2021).

fields_add.community: The Bank's completion report of 29 January 2021 sets out the audit finding the Panel relied on and adds the rest of the project's record. The audit of the Webuye interchange resettlement action plan revealed 13 small business tenants who had not been included in the plan, and recommended cash compensation of KES 20,000 each for loss of income and relocation or disturbance, computed as an average of three months of net income; all 13 mobile traders received that payment in April 2020. It also recommended building a market for the 52 mobile traders omitted from the 2011 plan; the Government committed to build it, the land was identified and the engineering design was in progress when the report was written. Three other road sections drew complaints to the Bank's grievance service. On the Kakamega to Webuye section a complainant alleged a fatal accident involving a worker on site, dog attacks on workers in the contractor's camp, sexual exploitation and abuse of school girls by workers, and summary dismissal of workers who raised grievances. A Bank mission confirmed that there had been a fatal accident on site involving the operator of an excavator, that it had been reported to the police at the time, that the police took over the case, and that the Bank team followed up with the roads authority to ensure the family of the deceased was compensated under Kenyan law. It confirmed that the contractor kept five dogs for security, that they had roamed freely in the camp until workers complained and were then locked in kennels, and that one worker had been bitten and was treated at a local hospital. The allegation of sexual exploitation was investigated and could not be substantiated: the report records that children's officers, heads of schools and community leaders all said there had been no reports of abuse of children by workers. The allegation of summary dismissals could not be confirmed and the report says it appeared not to be true, since no member of the grievance committee or employee of the consultant or contractor who was interviewed knew of a worker dismissed for complaining. On the Athi River to Machakos section, compensation of affected people at the Gimu interchange was delayed while government agencies authenticated who was eligible, after the corridor was realigned to fit both the Standard Gauge Railway and the road widening and avoid double payment; some affected people complained to the Bank and that case was still open when the report was written. On the Bachuma Gate to Maji ya Chumvi contract one person's compensation was held in an escrow account with the National Land Commission while two families disputed ownership of the parcel in court. A further request for inspection on the project was submitted to the Inspection Panel and was not registered; the Panel issued a notice of non-registration on 13 April 2022.

fields_add.community: The World Bank's completion report of 26 June 2019 for the same project, P108143, records the outcome. The dam and its ancillary works were designed to keep physical displacement to a minimum, and only six households needed relocation under the Replacement Housing Program; their replacement houses were completed and used. Across the contract work areas there were 2,798 affected households, of whom 2,615 had received compensation by closing, 93 per cent of the target. Disbursement of compensation was still going on when the project closed on 31 December 2018, with 183 cases, 6.5 per cent, outstanding; M 59.36 million had been paid and M 3.82 million, 6 per cent, was still to be paid. The Metolong Authority judged that more than 107 of the outstanding cases could be completed without difficulty. The remaining 76 were 36 cases in dispute in the courts and 40 cases of people who had migrated to South Africa or elsewhere. The report attributes the outstanding disputes to arguments over who owned the affected property, to the compensation amounts, which in some cases led people not to claim the money due to them, and to the difficulty of finding people who had moved away. The main cause of the delay was compensation tied to rural electrification work, whose scope grew from 35 villages to 80 and which was carried out late in the programme. Of the affected households, 550 were headed by women and almost 10 per cent of household heads were disabled, so the compensation programme added specific measures for them. The report also records that errors were made in valuing assets, which led to compensation requirements being overestimated; the valuation methods were then adjusted, disputes arose, compensation was delayed, and the ombudsman had to be brought in to reach a settlement. In 2012 the dam contractor began construction and blasting without an approved environmental protection plan, a blasting plan, a blasting method statement, a mining permit, an approved evacuation plan or a satisfactory dilapidation survey; some activities were suspended, and complaints followed an uncontrolled blast in August 2012. There were ten fatalities during implementation of the Metolong programme, all of which the report says were properly reported and settled under Lesotho's Labour Code. A livelihood restoration programme trained the two affected communities of Ratau and Motanasela in poultry, pig-keeping, value chains, group dynamics, conflict resolution and social cohesion, and both communities set up trust funds managed by Standard Lesotho Bank. Implementation of the resettlement action plan was not finished when the project closed, and the Bank said it would keep supervising until the end of 2019. In March 2019 the government extended the Metolong Authority's mandate to October 2019 to finish the compensation payments and the livelihood work, and made a budget provision of M 1,800,000 for pending compensation. In February 2026 GroundUp reported that the communities around the dam still had no tap water, and quoted a spokesperson for the Machache Water Supply Movement saying that they host the project and that it is on their land.
fields_add.confidence_note: The P-number, the credit and grant numbers, the 2,798 affected households, the 183 outstanding compensation cases, the six households relocated, the ten fatalities, the 2012 blasting without permits and the involvement of the ombudsman all come from the World Bank's own completion report of 26 June 2019 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. The review repeats the six households, the 2,615 of 2,798 compensated and the 550 female-headed households, but omits the ten fatalities, the blasting without permits, the uncontrolled blast of August 2012 and the ombudsman. The report gives no cause for any of the ten deaths and does not say when or where they happened or who the dead were, so none is counted here. The Bank's figures and the Metolong Authority's figures reported four months earlier do not match exactly: the report counts 2,798 affected households and 183 outstanding compensation cases at 31 December 2018, against the 2,786 affected families and 247 unpaid reported for August 2018. GroundUp's February 2026 report that the host communities still have no tap water is the independent account; it gives the dam's cost as R7 billion and names the World Bank among the lenders, and carries no figures on compensation or resettlement.
fields_add.killed_note: The World Bank's completion report of 26 June 2019 states that there were ten fatalities during implementation of the Metolong Dam and Water Supply Programme, and that all of them were properly reported and settled following the requirements of Lesotho's Labour Code. The sentence stands in the report's paragraph on the grievance redress mechanism. The report gives no cause, no date, no place and no identity for any of the ten, and settlement under the Labour Code is not a statement that the works caused the deaths, so none is counted. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of the report omits the ten fatalities entirely.
